clue.text: Knocked back food — a French dory, filleted — and wine

indicators.note: a drink knocked back is tipped up and downed, so these letters are turned round to read backwards

parts.note: grub is slang for food
un is the French for a

indicators.note: a filleted fish has its insides removed, leaving only the outer skin of the word

parts.note: the first and last letters of the fish's name

explanation.surface: Someone wolfs down a fish supper, a filleted John Dory, with a glass of wine alongside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' looks like it goes with the wine, but it turns the food round. A dory is a sea fish; filleting it keeps only its outside letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Burgundy is a French region whose red and white vintages are known by its name, so it is a type of the drink.

clue.text: Unpleasant to live with poet around

indicators.note: one thing placed around another encloses it, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: a bard is a poet
to be is to exist or live

explanation.surface: A complaint that a poet makes a disagreeable housemate.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'Unpleasant to live with' one phrase about a flatmate; the definition is only the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: A barbed remark is cutting and hurtful, so the adjective describes something nasty or hostile in tone.

clue.text: Direct section of Cairo bus trip

indicators.note: a section is a slice cut from something longer, so the letters are a run lifted out of the words that follow

parts.note: the run starts near the end of the city name and ends at the start of the last word

explanation.surface: Someone is told to take one leg of a bus journey through Cairo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Direct' reads as a verb telling you where to go, but it is an adjective here, as in a robust or direct reply.
explanation.definitionFit: A robust response is forthright and vigorous, which overlaps with being straightforward and blunt in manner.

clue.text: Everyman's in a tumult, wildly offering threat

indicators.note: acting wildly is acting without order, so the letters are thrown into a new arrangement

parts.note: the setter speaking of himself as I'm
taken as written

explanation.surface: The setter confesses to being in an uproar, lashing out with menaces.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's name stands for the first person, so Everyman's is I'M. It sits in the tumult and the whole lot is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: An ultimatum is a final demand backed by a stated penalty, so it is a form of warning or menace.

clue.text: Losing potency, facing defeat in struggle

indicators.note: things in a struggle are thrown about and tangled, so the letters land in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A fighter weakening as a loss in the contest looms.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a boxer flagging; the potency is really caffeine being taken out of coffee.
explanation.definitionFit: Removing caffeine from coffee or tea strips the drink of its stimulating kick, a witty take on weakening.

clue.text: Primarily vulgar, scornful, insulting gestures (not suave)?

definitions.text: Primarily vulgar, scornful, insulting gestures (not suave)

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so each word gives up its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of each of the six words

explanation.surface: A description of rude, mocking hand signals that no smooth operator would make.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay. A V-sign, two fingers raised with the palm inward, is an obscene gesture in Britain, like the middle finger.
explanation.definitionFit: Two raised fingers with the knuckles outward is a coarse British gesture of contempt, exactly the rude signal described.

clue.text: Scandalous, hearing about the Third Man?

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes round the other

parts.note: Kim Philby, the spy, was dubbed the Third Man of the Cambridge spy ring

indicators.note: what is heard is judged by sound, so letters are written that sound like a phrase

parts.note: saying I see is saying you hear and understand; the two letters sound the same

explanation.surface: Gossip about a lurid trial involving the Third Man of film or espionage fame.
explanation.walkthrough: The Third Man suggests the Orson Welles film, but here it is Kim Philby, a British double agent for the Soviets. 'I see' sounds like the letters I C.
explanation.definitionFit: Spicy gossip is racy and titillating, the colloquial word for something mildly shocking or improper.

clue.text: Most of singers getting hot drink, shortly, for composer

indicators.note: most of something is the greater part of it, so the word loses some of its letters
shortly means briefly, so the word is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: the last four of its seven letters, which is most of them
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap
wine with its last letter removed

explanation.surface: Most of a choir, given a hot drink, are soon ready to sing a composer's work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most of' here keeps four of seven letters, a bare majority, dropping SIN from the front.
explanation.definitionFit: George Gershwin was the American who wrote Rhapsody in Blue and Porgy and Bess, a famous writer of music.

clue.text: Those whereby duty is getting into going without?

definitions.text: Those whereby duty is getting into going without

indicators.note: getting into something means entering it, so one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: sans is an old word for without, from French
one's part is one's role or duty

explanation.surface: A question about people who treat obligation as part of living without comforts.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is definition and wordplay: ancient Spartans put duty first and lived austerely, and the wordplay puts duty inside a word for without.
explanation.definitionFit: Citizens of ancient Sparta were famed for discipline, self-denial and a frugal life, which is why austere now means spartan.

clue.text: Increasing power, Virgin Queen to gain sway

indicators.note: to sway is to rock and move about, so the letters shift into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the queen's royal cipher
taken as written

explanation.surface: Elizabeth I, the Virgin Queen, growing in strength and influence.
explanation.walkthrough: The Virgin Queen is a title of Elizabeth I, but here the words split: Virgin as written and Queen as ER. 'sway' looks like a noun meaning influence.
explanation.definitionFit: Reinvigorating something gives it fresh energy and vigour, restoring and boosting its strength.

clue.text: Heartless to steal books; sick to destroy covers

parts.note: to rob is to steal
OT, the Old Testament, is the usual crossword books

indicators.note: destroying a thing's covers strips off its outside, leaving only the inner part

parts.note: the word with its first and last letters stripped

explanation.surface: A vandal callous enough to steal books and, feeling ill, wreck their bindings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartless' could signal dropping middle letters, but it is the definition; the stripping instruction comes at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Something robotic acts mechanically, without feeling or warmth, as a machine with no emotions would.

clue.text: Baedeker: it really captures Red Sea land

indicators.note: to capture is to hold inside, so the letters are held within the words before it

parts.note: the run starts at the tail of the guidebook's name

explanation.surface: A review praising how well a travel guidebook conveys a country on the Red Sea.
explanation.walkthrough: Baedeker is a famous series of German travel guidebooks, hence the italics.
explanation.definitionFit: Eritrea is an East African country whose coastline runs along the Red Sea, so it is a nation bordering that water.

clue.text: Seconds before games return to racecourse

indicators.note: to return is to go back the way you came, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a second
PE, physical education, is school games

explanation.surface: Moments before a sporting event, people head back to the races.
explanation.walkthrough: PE is physical education, games lessons in a British school. Epsom is the Surrey racecourse that hosts the Derby.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsom Downs is a famous English horse-racing venue, so the town's name stands for the track.

clue.text: I'm surprised and tense, wearing expensive headgear

indicators.note: whatever is worn goes around the wearer, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: fancy can mean high-priced, and a hat is headgear
T is the grammar abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: Someone startled and anxious in a pricey hat, perhaps at a smart wedding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tense' looks like an adjective for being nervous, but it is the grammatical term, abbreviated to one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Fancy that! is a set exclamation of astonishment, so it can stand in for saying one is taken aback.

clue.text: Partitioned while trembling, trembling

definitions.note: the second 'trembling', used as a noun

indicators.note: something trembling is shaking about, so its letters are jolted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A nervous person divided off, shaking and shaking.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated word does two jobs: the first signals the rearrangement, the second is the definition, read as a noun meaning a fit of shaking.
explanation.definitionFit: Trepidation once meant literally quivering or tremulous agitation, and now means fearful nervousness.

clue.text: Diligent lasses find autocue's failing regularly

indicators.note: dropping out at regular intervals means every other letter goes missing

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth letters and so on

explanation.surface: Hard-working young women find the teleprompter keeps breaking down.
explanation.walkthrough: An autocue is a teleprompter that scrolls a presenter's script. 'Diligent lasses' reads as one phrase, but only the first word is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An assiduous worker shows careful, persistent attention and effort, the same industrious quality.

clue.text: Very bad to see yours truly excluded from biomedical engineering

indicators.note: engineering is building and rebuilding, so the letters are reconstructed in a new order
what is excluded is shut out, so some letters are removed from the longer word

parts.note: yours truly is the speaker, me
the word with its fourth and fifth letters taken away

explanation.surface: A scientist complains at being left out of a medical engineering project.
explanation.walkthrough: 'biomedical engineering' reads as a field of study, but the second word is the signal to rearrange what is left after the removal.
explanation.definitionFit: Diabolic means devilish, so it describes something extremely wicked or dreadful.

clue.text: Uppishness seen as Southern aristocrat topless, Derby scandalised

indicators.note: without a top, the word loses its first letter

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for southern

indicators.note: someone scandalised is thrown into upset, so the letters are disturbed into a new order

parts.note: a nob is slang for a toff, a person of high class
the name with its first letter dropped

explanation.surface: A haughty Southern lord shocks the racing crowd at the Derby by going bare-chested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topless' looks attached to the aristocrat, but it acts on the next word. The Derby is England's famous flat horse race at Epsom.
explanation.definitionFit: Snobbery is looking down on those thought socially inferior, the same airs as being uppity.

clue.text: 'Shameful' gin cocktail: not promising to get one in

indicators.note: a cocktail is a mixture, so the letters are mixed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: getting something in means taking it inside, so a piece is put within another

parts.note: ominous means threatening, the opposite of promising
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A gin cocktail branded disgraceful by someone dreading being asked to buy a round.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'Shameful' look like a review of the drink; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An ignominious defeat brings public disgrace and humiliation, so the word means disgraceful.

clue.text: Judge's drawn Nigella oddly

indicators.note: taking things oddly means picking the odd-numbered positions only

parts.note: the first, third, fifth letters and so on across both words

explanation.surface: A judge who has sketched Nigella Lawson, the TV cook, in a peculiar way.
explanation.walkthrough: Shylock's 'A Daniel come to judgment' in The Merchant of Venice made the name a byword for a wise judge.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical prophet's name means God is my judge, and after Shakespeare it is a byword for a shrewd arbiter.

clue.text: Uneven judge made criticisms, ignoring knight

parts.note: J is the abbreviation for judge

indicators.note: to ignore is to leave out of account, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: nagged means found fault persistently
N is the chess notation for knight

explanation.surface: An inconsistent judge carped at everyone except a knight of the realm.
explanation.walkthrough: In chess notation the knight is N, since K is taken by the king.
explanation.definitionFit: A jagged edge has rough, sharp points and notches rather than a smooth line, so it is irregular.

clue.text: Drink most of champagne, having briefly eaten out

indicators.note: most of a word is all but its last letter
briefly means cut short, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: bubbly is champagne, less its last letter

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or wrong, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the word short of its last letter

explanation.surface: A diner drinks most of the bubbly after a quick meal at a restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drink' looks like a verb ordering you to quaff the champagne; it is the noun definition. Bubbly is a casual name for champagne.
explanation.definitionFit: Bubble tea is a Taiwanese iced beverage with chewy tapioca pearls, so it is a kind of beverage.

clue.text: What's found in bathroom of India, ultimately?

definitions.text: What's found in bathroom of India, ultimately

parts.note: loo is an informal British word for a toilet or bathroom

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so each word gives up its final letter

parts.note: the final letter of each word

explanation.surface: A query about what turns up in an Indian bathroom, in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay. The answer is the plant-fibre bath sponge, from a gourd grown in India among other places.
explanation.definitionFit: A loofa, usually spelt loofah, is a dried gourd skeleton used as a scrubbing sponge in the bath.

clue.text: Finally performed ceremonial dance somewhere in Asia

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the last letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word
the haka is the Maori war dance performed by New Zealand's rugby team

explanation.surface: A ritual dance is at last staged somewhere on the Asian continent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally performed' reads as 'at last staged', but it only gives the closing letter of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: Dhaka is the capital city of Bangladesh, a place in South Asia, so the vague phrase points at it.

clue.text: Told a story? Have a little rest

parts.note: telling a story can mean telling a fib
to own is to have

explanation.surface: A storyteller finishes a tale and is told to take a short nap.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark splits the clue at the wrong place: 'Have' belongs with the first half, and the definition is only the last three words.
explanation.definitionFit: A lie-down is a short spell lying on a bed or sofa to recover, a brief nap or breather.

clue.text: Mostly insincere, no good and a bit of a chore

indicators.note: mostly means all but a little, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: ironic, saying the opposite of what one means, less its last letter
NG is the standard abbreviation for no good

explanation.surface: A grumble that some task is half-hearted, useless and rather tedious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a bit of a chore' sounds like a mild complaint, but it is the definition: one particular household task.
explanation.definitionFit: Pressing clothes with a hot iron is one of the routine household jobs people dread, so it is an example.

clue.text: Deadly reptile on island: my God!

parts.note: a cay is a small low island or reef
Man! is an exclamation of surprise, like my God!

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in horror on spotting a dangerous reptile on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cayman Islands make 'island' tempting as part of the answer's place-name sense, but the definition is the animal, also spelt caiman.
explanation.definitionFit: A cayman is a Central and South American relative of the alligator, a toothy predatory reptile.

clue.text: Encourages a boy to find something to eat

parts.note: eggs on, urges
taken as written
a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: A parent urges a youngster to go and forage for a snack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Encourages' looks like a plain verb, but the setter wants the word from 'egg on', to urge.
explanation.definitionFit: Egg salad is a dish of chopped boiled eggs and mayonnaise, a common sandwich filling and meal.
